analysis.one_liner: Lets generic drug makers sue brand-name companies that refuse to sell them samples needed for FDA approval testing.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan CREATES Act cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee in June 2018 and sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended — it never got a floor vote, despite 30 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies developing cheaper generic or biosimilar copies of a drug need samples of the original product to run the FDA-required comparison tests. Some brand-name manufacturers refuse to sell those samples — often citing strict safety distribution programs — which delays cheaper competitors from reaching the market. This bill would let the blocked generic developer sue in federal court to force the sale of samples at market price, with fees and penalties if the brand company stalls.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who would get lower-cost generics and biosimilars sooner, and taxpayers and insurers who fund prescription drug purchases. Generic drug developers also gain a faster, cheaper path to FDA approval.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and taxpayers facing high drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Brand-name manufacturers sometimes refuse to sell sample quantities of an approved drug to generic developers, in some cases citing risk-management safety restrictions, which blocks the testing needed for FDA approval [S3].

The FDA's drug-review director testified that some manufacturers use these safety programs and distribution restrictions as reasons not to sell samples, causing delays in getting generics on the market, and the agency has received many inquiries from generic developers unable to obtain samples [S3].

The bill lets the generic developer sue the brand company; if it wins, a court orders the samples delivered and can award attorney's fees plus a monetary penalty large enough to deter the brand company from stalling others, capped at the brand's revenue on that drug during the delay [S3].
The bill also lets the FDA approve comparable-but-different safety programs for generic drugs, so brands cannot endlessly stall negotiations over a single shared safety system [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, which would lose some of the extra monopoly revenue they earn each month a generic is delayed. There is also a potential safety cost: samples sold for testing would fall outside the brand drug's strict safety program, and the brand company's liability for the developer's handling is limited.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers with extended monopolies

drawbacks.text: The bill requires the FDA to authorize samples for drugs under strict safety programs, with protections only 'comparable' to the brand's program — a trade-off that could slightly weaken safety controls around drugs with serious risks [S3].
Brand companies would not be liable for harm arising from a generic developer's failure to follow adequate safeguards when transporting, using, or disposing of the covered product [S3].
The bill is narrow: it only addresses the withheld-samples tactic, leaving many other strategies brand companies use to delay generic competition untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — faster entry of lower-cost generics on high-priced drugs — is real and directed at a documented delay tactic, and the safety trade-off is hedged with FDA authorization requirements. But the bill is a targeted fix for one delay tactic, not a broad solution to drug prices, and the delayed-safety-program route is the part of the design an honest supporter would acknowledge carries risk.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it in June 2018 and put it on the Senate's general calendar, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in April 2017 by Senator Leahy with a bipartisan group of senators including Grassley, Klobuchar, Lee, and Cruz, and drew 30 cosponsors (15 Republicans, 14 Democrats, 1 Independent) [S1, S3, S4].
The Senate Judiciary Committee ordered the bill favorably reported in June 2018, and Senator Grassley reported it with an amendment on June 21, 2018 [S1, S5].
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 482) on June 21, 2018 — the queue of bills awaiting floor time — where it sat with no further action [S5].
No vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the sample-withholding tactic that extends their monopoly pricing for the life of the 115th Congress. Patients and insurers continued paying the higher prices that come with delayed generic competition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept extended monopolies

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and reported it out of committee favorably with an amendment in June 2018.

for.name: 30 senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support in both the committee and the full Senate.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill, which sat on the Senate calendar for over six months, to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Manufacturers of brand-name drugs and biological products
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would undermine drug safety programs and expose manufacturers to liability; it lobbied against the measure throughout the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan from the start: 15 Republicans, 14 Democrats, and 1 Independent cosponsored, and the bill was reported out of the Judiciary Committee by its Republican chairman with a Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: These companies had used safety distribution restrictions and refusal to sell samples to keep cheaper generics off the market longer; the bill would let generic developers sue to force sample sales and penalize stalling, cutting the extra months or years of monopoly revenue.

Developers would get a court path to obtain the samples they need for FDA-required testing, speeding their products to market; their business of selling cheaper copies runs alongside patients' interest in lower prices.
